subject: feminism
title: Second Wave (c. 1963–1982): the personal is political
dek: After the vote, the house. Then a public argument that housework, sex, pay, and who counted were already politics.

thumb.alt: Studio portrait of Betty Friedan, facing right, wearing a dark collared top and a coin necklace, 1960.

hero.alt: Women marching down a Washington, D.C. street on 26 August 1970, carrying banners reading Women Demand Equality and GWU Women’s Liberation.
hero.caption: Women’s Strike for Equality, Washington, D.C., 26 August 1970 — fifty years after the Nineteenth Amendment. The banners are local (George Washington University Women’s Liberation among them). This is not the Fifth Avenue photograph. The date is national; the street is one city.
hero.credit: Warren K. Leffler / U.S. News & World Report collection, Library of Congress / public domain

honesty: “Second wave” is a later Anglo-American classroom name, not what most of the people in this capsule called themselves. The dates are a convenience: The Feminine Mystique (1963) at one end, the Equal Rights Amendment’s extended ratification deadline (30 June 1982) at the other. The United States is the spine because the numbering is. Other countries’ 1960s–70s feminisms are contemporaneous — not a seating chart of copies.

timeline.label: Mystique / pay
timeline.detail: Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique. The Equal Pay Act the same year. A bestseller and a statute; neither was the whole cause.

timeline.label: NOW
timeline.detail: National Organization for Women founded in Washington, 30 June, after a conference of status-of-women commissions. Friedan first president; Pauli Murray among the founders.

timeline.label: Atlantic City
timeline.detail: New York Radical Women protest the Miss America pageant, 7 September. Freedom Trash Can. No fire.

timeline.label: Books / strike / Ruskin
timeline.detail: Sexual Politics; The Dialectic of Sex; Notes from the Second Year; Our Bodies, Ourselves as newsprint; Women’s Strike for Equality, 26 August; first UK Women’s Liberation conference at Ruskin College.

timeline.label: Statute / Roe
timeline.detail: Title IX in the Education Amendments of 1972 (signed 23 June). ERA sent to the states. Ms. magazine. Roe v. Wade decided 22 January 1973.

timeline.label: Combahee / Houston
timeline.detail: Combahee River Collective Statement (April). National Women’s Conference in Houston (November), and a conservative Pro-Family rally in the same city.

timeline.label: Deadline
timeline.detail: ERA ratification deadline expires 30 June, three states short. Reagan already in office; Thatcher since 1979. The later names — third wave, intersectionality — are not yet the ones in use.

listen.title: Roe v. Wade — oral argument (Oyez)
listen.note: Audio of the Supreme Court argument (1971) and reargument (1972), with the 22 January 1973 opinion. This is the case, not a documentary about it.

read.title: Carol Hanisch — “The Personal Is Political” (1970), with the author’s 2006 note
read.note: The essay as printed in Notes from the Second Year. Hanisch’s introduction is the useful correction: she did not title it; Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt did.

read.title: Combahee River Collective Statement (April 1977)
read.note: The 1977 text. BlackPast hosts it; the statement itself is the source. Primary authors later named: Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, Demita Frazier.

read.title: National Organization for Women — Statement of Purpose (1966)
read.note: NOW’s own posting of the founding statement, co-authored in part by Pauli Murray.

read.title: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 — U.S. Department of Justice
read.note: The statutory text. It is a sex-discrimination rule for federally funded education, not a sports law that later grew a statute.

read.title: Education Amendments of 1972, Public Law 92-318 (86 Stat. 235) — GovInfo
read.note: The enrolled law Nixon signed on 23 June 1972. Title IX is in this PDF (86 Stat. 373), not a separate act.

read.title: Roe v. Wade, 410 U.S. 113 (1973) — Legal Information Institute
read.note: The U.S. Reports text of the decision. Open transcription of the bound volume; not a summary article.

read.title: Betty Friedan — The Feminine Mystique (W. W. Norton, 1963)
read.note: Library of Congress catalog record. The book is still in copyright; this is the record, not a full text.

read.title: Our Bodies Ourselves — the collective’s own history of the book
read.note: How a 1969 Boston workshop became 1970 newsprint (Women and Their Bodies) and then the book. Institutional memory, not a scan of the first edition.

fun_fact.title: There was no fire on the boardwalk
fun_fact.text: On 7 September 1968, New York Radical Women put bras, girdles, high heels, curlers, and women’s magazines into a “Freedom Trash Can” outside the Miss America pageant in Atlantic City. They asked the city for a permit to burn the contents. The permit was refused: the boardwalk is wood. Nothing was burned. Newspapers, then Art Buchwald’s column, reported a bra-burning anyway. The trash can is the event. The bonfire is the copy.

glossary.explain: A later Anglo-American label for a span of feminist organizing roughly from the early 1960s through the early 1980s. Most people in it did not use the phrase at the time. It is a filing system, not a membership card.

A later weather report for organized U.S. feminism between the vote and the 1960s: the coalition that had fought for suffrage thinned. It describes one public current going quiet. It does not mean women stopped working, studying, or arguing.

Friedan’s name for the postwar middle-class story that a woman’s fulfillment was husband, children, and house. She treated it as an ideology with a sales force — magazines, advertising, experts — not as a private mood.

glossary.term: the problem that has no name
glossary.explain: Friedan’s phrase in The Feminine Mystique for the dissatisfaction of college-educated housewives who had done what they were told and still felt empty. It named a specific class of unhappiness. It did not name every woman’s.
Betty Friedan’s 1963 book, published by W. W. Norton. A survey of her Smith College classmates and a polemic against the house-as-destiny. A public door. Not a census of American women.
American writer (1921–2006). The Feminine Mystique (1963); first president of NOW (1966). She later used the phrase “lavender menace” about lesbians in the movement — a split, not a footnote.
U.S. statute signed 10 June 1963. It required equal pay for equal work on the basis of sex, with exceptions. A workplace law in the same year as Friedan’s book. Enforcement was another matter.

glossary.term: Presidential Commission on the Status of Women
glossary.explain: A federal commission created by John F. Kennedy in 1961; Eleanor Roosevelt chaired it until her death in 1962. State commissions followed. NOW was founded at their Third National Conference in 1966.

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. It barred employment discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. The word “sex” is in the statute. Early Equal Employment Opportunity Commission practice did not treat it as equal to race.
U.S. civil-rights statute. Title VII is the employment title. The Act is the legal floor many workplace feminists stood on; it is not itself a feminist manifesto.
Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, created to enforce Title VII. NOW’s founding complaint was that the Commission was not treating sex discrimination as a real mandate.

National Organization for Women, founded 30 June 1966 in Washington, D.C. Twenty-eight founders; Betty Friedan first president. A civil-rights-style organization for sex equality: lawsuits, lobbying, later the 1970 strike. Not the same thing as women’s liberation small groups.

American lawyer, writer, and later Episcopal priest (1910–1985). Co-founder of NOW; co-author of its Statement of Purpose. “Jane Crow” was her name for the combined racial and sex caste she had already analyzed.
Pauli Murray’s term for the system that constrained Black women by race and sex together — not two separate queues.
NOW’s 1966 founding statement. It begins by defining the organization’s purpose as bringing women into “full participation in the mainstream of American society now.” Pauli Murray helped write it.

Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. A major civil-rights organization of the early 1960s. Several white women who later became women’s-liberation organizers had been trained in its discipline — and in its sex hierarchy.

The 1960s student and antiwar left, especially Students for a Democratic Society and related groups. A school for organizing. Also a place many women learned they were expected to type, staple, and wait.
Civil-rights organizer. With Mary King she wrote the 1965 memo “Sex and Caste,” circulated in SNCC, naming sex hierarchy inside the movement.
Civil-rights organizer; co-author, with Casey Hayden, of the 1965 SNCC memo “Sex and Caste.”

Memo by Casey Hayden and Mary King, November 1965, circulated in SNCC. It compared the position of women in the movement to a caste. A document from inside civil rights, before NOW’s founding conference.

A women’s-liberation method: a small group speaks from its own lives, then looks for the pattern. Kathie Sarachild presented “A Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising” in 1968. The point was analysis, not therapy — a distinction Carol Hanisch had to keep defending.
New York Radical Women member. She presented “A Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising” at the first national women’s-liberation conference, Chicago, November 1968.
Kathie Sarachild’s 1968 outline of consciousness-raising as a political method, later printed in Notes from the Second Year.
Early women’s-liberation group, formed in New York in 1967. Among those involved: Shulamith Firestone, Carol Hanisch, Robin Morgan, Kathie Sarachild. It organized the 1968 Miss America protest.

Phrase attached to Carol Hanisch’s 1969 memo when Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt printed it in Notes from the Second Year (1970) and gave it that title. Hanisch has said she did not name the paper. The claim: what gets called a private problem — housework, sex, abortion, shame — is a power relation.
Women’s-liberation organizer; New York Radical Women. She helped organize the 1968 Miss America protest. Her 1969 memo, titled by others in 1970, is the usual source for “the personal is political.”
1970 women’s-liberation anthology edited by Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt. It printed Hanisch’s memo under the title “The Personal Is Political,” and Sarachild’s consciousness-raising program.
Feminist writer and editor. Co-editor, with Firestone, of Notes from the Second Year. Co-founder of New York Radical Feminists.
Writer and organizer (1945–2012). New York Radical Women, Redstockings, New York Radical Feminists. The Dialectic of Sex (1970). Co-editor of Notes from the Second Year.

Shulamith Firestone’s 1970 book (William Morrow). A radical materialist argument: pregnancy and the sex class built on it are the base; cybernetic reproduction is a speculative horizon. Not a NOW pamphlet.

Writer and sculptor (1934–2017). Sexual Politics (1970), drawn from her Columbia dissertation: literature and theory as a record of patriarchy. Time put her on a cover; the fame was a trap as much as a platform.

Kate Millett’s 1970 book (Doubleday). Close reading of literary patriarchy — Lawrence, Miller, Mailer, Genet — as political theory. One of 1970’s two brick-sized feminist books; Firestone’s was the other.
Radical feminist group formed in New York in 1969 (Firestone and Ellen Willis among the founders). Speak-outs, including on abortion. The name plays on “bluestocking” and red.
Writer and critic; co-founder of Redstockings. Later a voice in the late-1970s arguments over sexuality and pornography.
The small-group, often radical current of the late 1960s–70s, distinct from NOW’s organizational liberalism though people crossed. In Britain, Women’s Liberation Movement (WLM) is the usual name.

Demonstration at the Miss America pageant, Atlantic City, 7 September 1968, organized by New York Radical Women. Freedom Trash Can on the boardwalk; a “Women’s Liberation” banner inside the hall. About two hundred people. Not a bonfire.
The barrel on the Atlantic City boardwalk, 7 September 1968, into which protesters threw bras, girdles, heels, curlers, and women’s magazines. A permit to burn the contents was denied.
Writer and organizer. A principal organizer of the 1968 Miss America protest; the “No More Miss America” leaflet is associated with her. Later editor of Sisterhood Is Powerful (1970).
Anthology edited by Robin Morgan, 1970. A thick reader of the new movement, not a single line.

A pageant held in Atlantic City the same night as the 1968 Miss America contest, organized as a Black alternative to a white national symbol. A different project from the boardwalk protest, on the same date.
American humor columnist. After the 1968 Miss America protest he helped spread the bra-burning story that the boardwalk itself had not supplied.

Journalist and organizer. A public face of liberal feminism in the 1970s; a founding editor of Ms. magazine (1972). Women’s Action Alliance; National Women’s Political Caucus. The cameras could file her. The arguments behind her were already about who “woman” included.
Feminist magazine. A preview ran in New York magazine in December 1971; the first standalone issue is 1972. Gloria Steinem was a founding editor. “Ms.” as a courtesy title was part of the point.
Organization co-founded in 1971 (Steinem among the founders) to supply practical feminist resources. The 12 January 1972 Leffler photograph of Steinem is from one of its news conferences.
Founded 1971 to elect women and feminist-allied candidates. Among the conveners: Bella Abzug, Shirley Chisholm, Betty Friedan, Gloria Steinem.
New York congresswoman (elected 1970), lawyer, and a convener of the National Women’s Political Caucus. Later a co-chair of the National Women’s Conference in Houston, 1977.

Brooklyn congresswoman, elected 1968 — the first Black woman in the U.S. House. She sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 1972. A convener of the National Women’s Political Caucus. Unbought and Unbossed (1970) is her campaign book and slogan.
Shirley Chisholm’s 1970 book, and the slogan of her campaigns. The phrase is hers, not a later caption.

Actions on 26 August 1970, the fiftieth anniversary of the Nineteenth Amendment, called by NOW and joined by a wider coalition. A Fifth Avenue march in New York; sister actions in other cities, including Washington, D.C. Friedan had asked for a strike. What the cameras got was mostly a march.

Women’s health book that began as a 1969 Boston workshop and 1970 newsprint (Women and Their Bodies) from the group later called the Boston Women’s Health Book Collective. New England Free Press, then a 1973 Simon & Schuster edition. The point was that women could know their own anatomy without waiting for a gatekeeper.
The Boston group that produced Our Bodies, Ourselves. A workshop, then a pamphlet, then a book that outlived the workshop.

Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, signed 23 June 1972. “No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” Sports became the public face. The text is broader. In 2002 the provision was renamed the Patsy T. Mink Equal Opportunity in Education Act.
Public Law 92-318, signed by Richard Nixon on 23 June 1972. Title IX is one title inside this law. Nixon’s signing statement did not dwell on the sex-discrimination provision.
Hawaii congresswoman. A principal House advocate of the sex-discrimination provision that became Title IX. The 2002 renaming of Title IX is after her.
Indiana senator. He introduced the Senate language that became Title IX, 28 February 1972.
U.S. president who signed the Education Amendments of 1972. The signing statement talked about higher education and busing. It did not sell Title IX as a women’s-sports law.

U.S. Supreme Court decision, 410 U.S. 113, announced 22 January 1973. Majority opinion by Harry Blackmun, 7–2. It held that the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause protected a right of privacy broad enough to include a woman’s decision to terminate a pregnancy, structured in trimesters, and struck down Texas’s criminal abortion statute. It was a constitutional holding, not a statute that “legalized abortion.” Overturned in 2022 by Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization.
Companion case to Roe, decided the same day (410 U.S. 179). It struck down Georgia’s more elaborate abortion restrictions. Read with Roe, not instead of it.
Supreme Court justice; author of the majority opinion in Roe v. Wade (1973).

Proposed U.S. constitutional amendment: equality of rights shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or any state on account of sex. Alice Paul introduced an ERA in 1923. Congress sent this version to the states on 22 March 1972. Original deadline 1979; extended to 30 June 1982. It fell three states short of 38.
Suffrage organizer; author of the original Equal Rights Amendment introduced in 1923. The 1972 ERA is her text’s descendant. She belongs to the earlier capsule; the amendment did not.

Conservative organizer (1924–2016). STOP ERA, from 1972, argued the amendment would strip protections from housewives, send women into the draft, and attack the family. The campaign is a fact of the 1970s, not a later invention.

Schlafly’s organization against ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment, from 1972. The stop-sign graphic is the image. The argument was that equality on paper would cost women the legal privileges of marriage and motherhood.

Phrase Betty Friedan used around 1969 for the fear that lesbians would discredit the movement. Reclaimed on 1 May 1970, when Radicalesbians disrupted the Second Congress to Unite Women in New York. The insult became a name.
Lesbian feminist group. They wrote “The Woman-Identified Woman” (1970) and staged the Lavender Menace action at the Second Congress to Unite Women, 1 May 1970.
Radicalesbians manifesto, 1970. It argued that lesbianism was a political position inside feminism, not a public-relations problem for NOW.
A current, not a single organization: the claim that intimate life with women, and a politics built from that fact, was central — not a side issue to be hidden for respectability.

Black feminist lesbian socialist collective in Boston, 1974–1980. Named for the June 1863 Combahee River Raid, in which Harriet Tubman helped lead a Union expedition that freed hundreds of enslaved people. Their April 1977 statement is the text this capsule slows down for.

Dated April 1977. It argues that racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression are interlocking, and that Black women’s politics have to start from that fact. It uses the phrase “identity politics” for a coalition that does not require anyone to stand aside. Later printings include a 1979 anthology edited by Zillah Eisenstein. Primary authors later named: Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, Demita Frazier.
Writer and organizer; co-founder of the Combahee River Collective; later of Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press. One of the three who later discussed authorship of the 1977 statement.
Organizer and writer; Barbara Smith’s sister; one of the three later named as primary authors of the Combahee River Collective Statement.
Organizer; one of the three later named as primary authors of the Combahee River Collective Statement.

In the Combahee statement, a name for politics that begin from one’s own structural position — Black, woman, lesbian, working-class — without treating those as separate queues. The later pejorative use of the phrase is not the 1977 use.

A current inside the era, not a later correction pasted on. National Black Feminist Organization (1973); Combahee (1974–80); writers including the Smiths, Frazier, and, late in the window, bell hooks. The who-counts problem returning in public.

Founded in New York in 1973 to address Black women’s position in both the women’s movement and Black politics. Combahee began among Boston women who had been in its orbit and wanted a more radical, socialist, lesbian-inclusive politics.
Abolitionist. The Combahee River Collective took its name from the 1863 Combahee River Raid she helped lead. The name is a claim of descent, not a 1970s photograph of her.
June 1863 Union raid on the Combahee River in South Carolina, with Harriet Tubman as a scout and leader, freeing hundreds of enslaved people. The 1970s collective borrowed the name on purpose.

Writer (Gloria Jean Watkins, 1952–2021). Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism (South End Press, 1981). Late in this capsule’s window: she is arguing with a movement that has already named itself, not founding NOW. She kept the name lowercase.

aliases: Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism
glossary.explain: bell hooks’s 1981 book. The title reaches back to Sojourner Truth’s 1851 Akron speech — and to the later refrain attached to it. In this archive that refrain’s history is in the First Wave capsule. The 1981 book is about Black women and the feminism that had trouble counting them.

Federally funded conference in Houston, 18–21 November 1977, following International Women’s Year. Delegates adopted a National Plan of Action (ERA, abortion, lesbian rights, minority women, and more). Three First Ladies appeared. A conservative Pro-Family rally met in Houston the same weekend.
United Nations designation for 1975. It produced a Mexico City conference and, in the U.S., a commission and the 1977 Houston meeting.
The 26-plank document adopted at Houston in 1977, recommendations to the President and Congress. A federal-room text. Combahee’s statement, months earlier, is a different genre of “we.”
U.S. First Lady in 1977. She appeared at the National Women’s Conference in Houston with Betty Ford and Lady Bird Johnson.
Former U.S. First Lady; ERA supporter. On the Houston stage, November 1977.
Former U.S. First Lady. On the Houston stage, November 1977, with Rosalynn Carter and Betty Ford.

Conservative gathering in Houston during the 1977 National Women’s Conference, associated with Schlafly and opponents of the ERA, abortion rights, and lesbian planks. Same city, same weekend, a different “family.”
Organization founded in New York in 1979. Part of the late-1970s turn toward pornography as a feminist target. The louder “sex wars” continue past this capsule’s 1982 line.
Mouvement de libération des femmes. French women’s-liberation current, named in the press around a 26 August 1970 demonstration at the Arc de Triomphe. Not a branch office of NOW.
Statement published in Le Nouvel Observateur, 5 April 1971, in which 343 women declared they had had abortions, then illegal in France. Simone de Beauvoir was among the signers.
French philosopher. The Second Sex (1949) is earlier than this capsule. She signed the Manifesto of the 343 in 1971. A predecessor and a contemporary, depending on which book you open.
Simone de Beauvoir’s 1949 book (Le Deuxième Sexe). A philosophical inventory of “woman” as Other. It is not a second-wave text; second-wave readers treated it as one anyway.

Trade-union college in Oxford. Site of the first British National Women’s Liberation Conference, 27 February–1 March 1970. Four opening demands: equal pay, equal education and opportunity, 24-hour nurseries, free contraception and abortion on demand.

Japanese women’s liberation of the early 1970s, from the English “women’s lib.” Tanaka Mitsu’s 1970 pamphlet Liberation from the Toilet is a founding text. Ribu Shinjuku Center (1972–77) was a shelter, clinic, and meeting place. A critique of the family system and of New Left sexism, not a translation of Friedan.
Japanese ribu organizer and writer. Liberation from the Toilet (便所からの解放), 1970. A founder of the Ribu Shinjuku Center.
Tanaka Mitsu’s 1970 ribu pamphlet. It attacked the treatment of women — including by men on the left — as a receptacle. The title is hers; it is not a metaphor invented for this capsule.
Women’s center and shelter in Shinjuku, Tokyo, 1972–1977. A ribu institution: housing, abortion and legal advice, a paper, a place to go.

Lü Hsiu-lien’s name for the feminism she promoted in 1970s Taiwan: a 8 March 1972 lecture at National Taiwan University’s law college, then the 1974 book 新女性主義. Slogans included “first a person, then a man or a woman.” This was under martial law, not under the U.S. numbering.

Taiwanese lawyer and writer (b. 1944). She introduced New Feminism in Taipei in the early 1970s after graduate study in the United States. Later vice president of the Republic of China (2000–2008). The later office is not this capsule; the 1974 book is.
Uprising at the Stonewall Inn, New York, June 1969. Gay liberation is a contemporaneous movement, not a subplot of NOW. Lesbian feminism sits in the overlap.

A word later attached, especially by Susan Faludi’s 1991 book Backlash, to the 1980s counter-movement: Reagan–Thatcher conservatism, anti-ERA organizing, a media story that feminism had gone too far. The word is 1991. The weather is already in this capsule’s last years.
Journalist. Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women (1991). A later name for the 1980s, written after this capsule’s dates.

aliases: Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women
glossary.explain: Susan Faludi’s 1991 book. Useful as a later diagnosis. It is not a 1977 source.
U.S. president from 20 January 1981. His first term is the American half of the conservative turn this capsule ends in.
British prime minister from 4 May 1979. The other English-speaking conservative date in the after.

A later name. Rebecca Walker’s “Becoming the Third Wave” appeared in Ms. in January 1992. This capsule stops before the name. The problems the name tried to hold — race, sexuality, culture, who “we” is — were already on the table.
Writer. Her 1992 Ms. essay “Becoming the Third Wave” is a usual starting citation for the phrase. It is after this capsule.
Rebecca Walker’s essay in Ms., January 1992. A later christening, not a 1982 event.

Legal-theoretical name coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989 for the way race and sex (and other structures) compound. Combahee had already stated interlocking oppressions in 1977. The word is later. The problem is not.
Legal scholar. “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989) is the usual origin of the word intersectionality. After this capsule; in conversation with it.

glossary.term: Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex
glossary.explain: Kimberlé Crenshaw’s 1989 article in the University of Chicago Legal Forum. The named origin of “intersectionality.”

glossary.term: Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization
glossary.explain: U.S. Supreme Court decision, 2022, that overruled Roe v. Wade. Not part of the 1963–82 span. Named here only as the later fate of a 1973 holding.

Postwar planned suburbs (Pennsylvania, New York, and others) associated with mass-produced houses and a racial boundary at the door. The 1958 photograph in this capsule is a house in Levittown, New York, made for House Beautiful. Architecture as a clue, not a biography of a resident.
American shelter magazine. The Gottscho-Schleisner Levittown negatives used here were shot for it in August 1958.

U.S. constitutional amendment, ratified 1920, barring denial of the vote on account of sex. The 1970 strike chose its fiftieth anniversary. What the amendment did not undo is in the First Wave capsule.
Later label for the suffrage-era public fights already treated in this archive’s Monday capsule of 16 August 2026. The who-counts problem did not end when the vote arrived.
U.S. president who created the Presidential Commission on the Status of Women in 1961. The commissions, not the Oval Office, are the useful fact here.
Major New Left student organization of the 1960s. A training ground and, for many women, a lesson in being asked to type.
Socialist-feminist organization founded in Chicago in 1969. Named here as one of the cities that was not New York.
Feminist conference in New York, 1 May 1970, where Radicalesbians staged the Lavender Menace action.
Village in New York State; 1848 convention site. In 1977 a torch was walked from there to Houston for the National Women’s Conference — a piece of first-wave theater reused as second-wave ceremony.
Ratified 1868. Roe’s majority located a right of privacy in its Due Process Clause. That reading is the 1973 holding; Dobbs rejected it in 2022.
French weekly. It published the Manifesto of the 343 on 5 April 1971.
New York publisher of The Feminine Mystique in 1963.
Taipei university. Lü Hsiu-lien lectured on New Feminism at its law college on 8 March 1972.
University in Washington, D.C. Its Women’s Liberation banner is readable in the 26 August 1970 photograph used as this capsule’s hero.
Lyndon B. Johnson Presidential Library in Austin. The 9 November 1975 Steinem photograph was taken at a women’s conference there.
Late-1960s current in Black politics emphasizing self-determination. Contemporaneous with women’s liberation; not scenery.
New York World-Telegram & Sun staff photographer. He made the 1960 Friedan portrait in this capsule.
U.S. News & World Report staff photographer. The 1970 Washington march and the 1977 Schlafly STOP ERA pictures in this capsule are his.
U.S. News & World Report staff photographer. The 25 January 1972 Chisholm portrait in this capsule is his.
White House / LBJ Library photographer. The 9 November 1975 Steinem picture is credited to him.
New York architectural photography firm. Their 1958 Levittown negatives, made for House Beautiful, are in the Library of Congress with no known copyright restrictions.
How the 1958 Gottscho catalog names the Levittown house in this capsule: a wife attached to a husband’s mailbox. The filing is the evidence.
American magazine. Staff photographs by Leffler, O’Halloran, and others, donated to the Library of Congress, are in the public domain under the deed of gift.
New York newspaper. Staff photographs donated to the Library of Congress, including Palumbo’s Friedan portrait, have no known restrictions.

sections.title: The vote, the doldrums, and a house with a name on the mailbox

blocks.text: The First Wave (c. 1848–1920) ended, in the United States, with a constitutional sentence about the vote. What followed, in the usual textbook weather report, is the doldrums: the suffrage coalition thinned, the Equal Rights Amendment that Alice Paul had already written sat in Congress, and a middle-class public story put women back in the house as if the house were a prize. The word “doldrums” is a later forecast. It describes one organized current going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended, and it does not mean every woman had been in that current.

Suburban domesticity had an architecture. Mass-produced houses, a car in the drive, a lawn that looked like a job. Magazines sold the picture. So did advertisers and a certain kind of expert. Friedan would call the picture the feminine mystique — a destiny with appliances. The picture was never a map of the country. Black women, working-class women, and anyone who had not been offered the delicate house were already in the workplace, already in other people’s kitchens, already counted as labor. The gap the First Wave left — who counted as the “woman” the movement was picturing — did not close in 1920. It went indoors and called itself normal.

blocks.alt: A two-story suburban house in Levittown, New York, with a car in the drive and young trees along a new lawn, 28 August 1958.
blocks.caption: Levittown, New York, 28 August 1958: the Mrs. Robert Berman house on Regent Lane, photographed for House Beautiful. The catalog files the resident as a wife of a mailbox. This is the architecture The Feminine Mystique would write against — and it was only ever one class of house.
blocks.credit: Gottscho-Schleisner Collection, Library of Congress / public domain

blocks.text: There was already law at the door of the 1960s. Kennedy’s Presidential Commission on the Status of Women (1961) produced reports and a string of state commissions. The Equal Pay Act arrived in 1963. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 named sex in employment. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission then had to decide whether that word was a mandate or a joke. The school many organizers came out of was not a commission. It was civil rights and the New Left: SNCC, the antiwar movement, Students for a Democratic Society. Casey Hayden and Mary King’s 1965 memo “Sex and Caste,” circulated in SNCC, is one document of what women learned there — how to run a meeting, and who was expected to take notes in it.

sections.title: A public spark, a method, and a street that would not stay private

blocks.text: Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique, published by W. W. Norton in 1963, is the public spark American memory keeps. It is not the cause. Friedan wrote about college-educated housewives and “the problem that has no name.” The book sold because a class of readers recognized themselves. Women who had never been offered that house did not need Friedan to tell them they were tired. Treat the book as a door that magazines could see. Do not treat it as the building.

blocks.alt: Betty Friedan in a 1960 studio portrait, three years before The Feminine Mystique.
blocks.caption: Betty Friedan, 1960 — three years before the book. Fred Palumbo’s World Telegram & Sun portrait is the face later filed with 1963. The useful date in the print is 1960: she is already a public person. The mystique had not yet been a bestseller.
blocks.credit: Fred Palumbo / New York World-Telegram & Sun Collection, Library of Congress / public domain

blocks.text: On 30 June 1966, at the Third National Conference of Commissions on the Status of Women in Washington, twenty-eight people founded the National Organization for Women. Friedan became president. Pauli Murray, who had already named “Jane Crow,” helped write the Statement of Purpose: women into the mainstream of American society now. NOW was built like a civil-rights organization — complaints to the EEOC, lawsuits, lobbying. It was one current. Women’s liberation small groups were another: New York Radical Women (1967), Redstockings (1969), Chicago Women’s Liberation Union, and dozens of unnamed living-room meetings. Consciousness-raising was the method. Kathie Sarachild put it on paper in 1968. You spoke from your own life until housework, sex, pay, and shame stopped looking like a private failure.

Carol Hanisch wrote a memo in February 1969 defending those meetings against the charge that they were therapy. When Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt printed it in Notes from the Second Year (1970), they titled it “The Personal Is Political.” Hanisch has said the title is theirs. The claim is the era’s: the home was already a political economy. So were abortion, heterosexuality, and the unpaid second shift.

How it showed: NOW, and the 26 August 1970 Women’s Strike for Equality on the Nineteenth Amendment’s fiftieth anniversary. Women’s liberation groups that would not be NOW. The Miss America protest of 7 September 1968 in Atlantic City — New York Radical Women, a Freedom Trash Can, a banner inside the hall, men kept off the action, no fire on a wooden boardwalk. The same night, a Miss Black America pageant ran in the same city as a different answer to a white national symbol. Our Bodies, Ourselves began as a 1969 Boston workshop and 1970 newsprint from the group later called the Boston Women’s Health Book Collective. Kate Millett’s Sexual Politics and Firestone’s The Dialectic of Sex both arrived in 1970. Ms. magazine’s first standalone issue is 1972; Gloria Steinem was a founding editor. Legislation, in the United States: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, signed 23 June — a sex-discrimination rule for federally funded education, with Patsy Mink in the House and Birch Bayh in the Senate; sports became the picture people could see. Roe v. Wade, 22 January 1973: a 7–2 Supreme Court, Harry Blackmun writing, held that the Fourteenth Amendment’s due-process privacy covered a woman’s decision to end a pregnancy, with a trimester framework, and struck down Texas’s criminal statute. It was a constitutional holding. It was not a law that “legalized abortion” in a sentence. Doe v. Bolton came down the same day.

blocks.alt: Gloria Steinem at a lectern, long hair and aviator glasses, speaking at a women’s conference at the LBJ Library, 9 November 1975.
blocks.caption: Gloria Steinem at the LBJ Library, 9 November 1975. The glasses and the microphone are how a movement got filed as a person. By 1975 the arguments behind the podium — class, race, lesbianism, who “Ms.” was for — were already the story.
blocks.credit: LBJ Library photo by Frank Wolfe / public domain (U.S. government work)

blocks.text: Black feminism is inside this span, not a footnote written later. The National Black Feminist Organization formed in 1973. The Combahee River Collective, in Boston from 1974, put a statement in April 1977. Lesbian feminism had already refused to wait: Radicalesbians’ “The Woman-Identified Woman,” and the Lavender Menace action at the Second Congress to Unite Women on 1 May 1970, answering Friedan’s slur by wearing it. By the late 1970s the arguments were also about pornography and about difference — Women Against Pornography dates to 1979 — and those fights run past the 1982 line this capsule uses as a date, not as a conclusion.

blocks.alt: Shirley Chisholm in patterned blouse and cat-eye glasses, photographed 25 January 1972 as she announced her presidential candidacy.
blocks.caption: Shirley Chisholm announcing a run for the Democratic presidential nomination, 25 January 1972. She had been in the House since 1969. A convener of the National Women’s Political Caucus, with Steinem, Friedan, and Bella Abzug. Electoral feminism is one street. It is not the only one.
blocks.credit: Thomas J. O’Halloran / U.S. News & World Report collection, Library of Congress / public domain

sections.title: Many names, then three places to slow down

blocks.text: A gallery of three portraits is the wrong picture. Name them, then stop treating the names as the era. Friedan, Steinem, Firestone, Millett. Pauli Murray at NOW’s founding. Shirley Chisholm in Congress and on a 1972 ballot. Bella Abzug. Patsy Mink and Birch Bayh on Title IX. Carol Hanisch and Kathie Sarachild on method. Robin Morgan on the boardwalk in 1968. Phyllis Schlafly on the other side of the ERA. Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, Demita Frazier on a 1977 statement. bell hooks in 1981, late, already arguing with a “women” that had been too small. Tanaka Mitsu in Tokyo. Lü Hsiu-lien in Taipei. The Miss America action as an event that does not belong to one face.

Slow down for three, as examples inside the field, not as the field. The Feminine Mystique as a public door. Consciousness-raising as a method. Combahee as the who-counts problem returning in public — the same problem the First Wave capsule left on the table, under a different name.

sections.title: A door, a circle, and a we that would not queue

blocks.text: The door: Friedan’s book gave a class of readers a plot in which their unhappiness was not a personal defect. Magazines could review that plot. Television could book it. NOW could walk through it into the EEOC’s office. The limitation is the same fact as the success. A feminism whose opening scene is a white suburban kitchen will treat everyone else as a later chapter. Working women, Black women, lesbians — they were not later. They were already there, poorly filed.

The circle: consciousness-raising made a technique out of that filing error. You did not begin with a program. You began with what had been called trivia — who does the dishes, who gets believed, who is afraid on the street — and you waited until the trivia had a structure. Hanisch’s memo is the defense of that wait. The New Left had said: those are personal problems; the revolution will fix them; type this stencil in the meantime. CR said the stencil was the revolution’s unfinished business. It could become its own trap: a room of people who already resembled each other, mistaking recognition for a census. The method does not excuse the room. It explains why the room felt like politics.

The we: the Combahee River Collective Statement, April 1977, is not an appendix to Steinem. A Black feminist lesbian socialist collective in Boston, named for Harriet Tubman’s 1863 raid, wrote that racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression lock together, and that they would not be asked to choose which liberation to stand in line for. “Identity politics,” in their usage, is the opposite of a veto. It is a starting position from which coalition might be possible because no one is required to disappear. Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, and Demita Frazier are the three who later talked about writing it. The statement is the collective’s. Four years later, bell hooks’s Ain’t I a Woman (1981) is late in this window on purpose: a book arguing with a movement that had already decided what “woman” sounded like. The title borrows a nineteenth-century question this archive has already complicated. The 1981 argument is new only if you were not listening.

sections.title: The same years, not a franchise

blocks.text: In France the press named a Mouvement de libération des femmes around a 26 August 1970 demonstration at the Arc de Triomphe. On 5 April 1971, Le Nouvel Observateur printed the Manifesto of the 343: women stating they had had abortions, Simone de Beauvoir among them. The Second Sex was already twenty years old. In Britain, the first National Women’s Liberation Conference met at Ruskin College, Oxford, 27 February–1 March 1970, and listed four demands: equal pay; equal education and opportunity; 24-hour nurseries; free contraception and abortion on demand. In Japan, ūman ribu was not a translation of a New York leaflet. Tanaka Mitsu’s Liberation from the Toilet (1970) went at the family system and at men on the left; the Ribu Shinjuku Center (1972–77) was a shelter and a clinic. In Taiwan, under martial law, Lü Hsiu-lien lectured on New Feminism at National Taiwan University on 8 March 1972 and published 新女性主義 in 1974: first a person, then a man or a woman. That is a 1970s feminism. It is not an Asian guest at an American table.

The same years, in the same cities, were also civil rights, Black Power, the antiwar movement, student revolt, and, after Stonewall in 1969, gay liberation. Women’s liberation came out of those rooms and fought in them. A capsule that treated those movements as scenery would be repeating the error it is trying to describe.

sections.title: A deadline, a backlash, and names that arrive late

blocks.alt: Stage at the National Women’s Conference in Houston, 19 November 1977, with a WOMAN banner, a torch, and a podium marked National Women’s Conference 1977.
blocks.caption: National Women’s Conference, Houston, 19 November 1977. A White House photograph: Rosalynn Carter with Betty Ford and Lady Bird Johnson. The banner says WOMAN as if the noun were settled. A conservative Pro-Family rally met in the same city that weekend. Combahee’s statement was already six months old.
blocks.credit: White House Staff Photographers / National Archives (NAID 176924) / public domain

blocks.text: Houston in November 1977 is one picture of a peak: a federally funded conference, a National Plan of Action, three First Ladies, a torch walked from Seneca Falls. It is also a picture of a split. The Plan included the ERA, abortion, lesbian rights, minority women. Opponents held their own rally. Phyllis Schlafly’s STOP ERA had been at work since 1972. On 4 February 1977 her people were already at the White House fence with stop-sign stickers. Congress had sent the Equal Rights Amendment to the states in 1972. The deadline, extended, expired on 30 June 1982, three states short of thirty-eight.

blocks.alt: Phyllis Schlafly smiling, a STOP ERA badge on her coat, with other demonstrators and a White House fence behind her, 4 February 1977.
blocks.caption: Phyllis Schlafly, STOP ERA, in front of the White House, 4 February 1977. The smile is part of the politics: a claim that housewives had a movement too. The ERA’s clock was already running.
blocks.credit: Warren K. Leffler / U.S. News & World Report collection, Library of Congress / public domain

blocks.text: Margaret Thatcher took office in May 1979. Ronald Reagan in January 1981. Susan Faludi would call the 1980s a backlash in a 1991 book of that name. The word is later. The weather is in these last years: an official mood that feminism had been tried, or had gone too far, or had been a coastal taste. Roe stood until Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization in 2022. That sentence is outside the era. It belongs here as a fate, not as a twist.

The door into what gets called the third wave is a later naming. Rebecca Walker’s “Becoming the Third Wave” is 1992, in Ms. Intersectionality, as a word, is Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989. Combahee did not need the word to state interlocking oppressions. The staircase — first the vote, then the rest, then a third flight — is the after. It is useful until it hides the people who were never on the stairs.
When a movement says the personal is political, whose personal is allowed to count as politics?
